<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   • Sparrow is a full‑stack, monorepo‑style API management platform.  
   • Frontends:  
     – Desktop client (Tauri + Rust + Svelte).  
     – Web client (Svelte + Vite).  
     – Design system / Storybook for UI components.  
   • Backends (external repos, orchestrated via Docker Compose):  
     – Auth service (NestJS + MongoDB).  
     – API service (NestJS + MongoDB + Kafka).  
     – Proxy/gateway service.  
   • Shared code (packages/@sparrow‑*): common DTOs, component libraries, utilities.

2. Analyze the file structure  
   • Top‑level folders:  
     – apps/@sparrow‑desktop, apps/@sparrow‑web, apps/@sparrow‑storybook  
     – packages/@sparrow‑common, @sparrow‑library, @sparrow‑support, etc.  
     – docker‑compose.yml for local infrastructure.  
     – .github/workflows for CI/CD pipelines.  
   • Monorepo pattern: share common code in “packages”, consume in “apps”.  
   • Separate Svelte/Vite configs per app, Cargo config under desktop for Rust/Tauri.  

3. Examine the README for technical stack  
   • Frontend: Svelte 3/4, Vite, Storybook.  
   • Desktop: Tauri + Rust for native shell + Svelte UI.  
   • Backend (not in this repo): NestJS, Mongoose (MongoDB), Kafka.  
   • Dev & deploy: Docker, Docker Compose, Yarn, Husky, GitHub Actions.

4. How to create the system design diagram  
   a. Main components (boxes):  
      • Desktop App (Tauri + Rust + Svelte)  
      • Web App (Svelte + Vite)  
      • Storybook/Design System (Component Library)  
      • Shared Packages (Common DTOs, UI, Types)  
      • API Gateway / Proxy Service  
      • Authentication Service  
      • API Service (business logic)  
      • Data Stores: MongoDB, Kafka  
      • External Services: GitHub OAuth, Canny, Mixpanel  
      • CI/CD (GitHub Actions workflows)  
      • Local Dev infra (Docker Compose)  

   b. Relationships & data flows (arrows):  
      • Desktop/Web → HTTP/WS → Proxy → Auth & API Services  
      • API Service ↔ MongoDB (CRUD)  
      • API Service ↔ Kafka (events)  
      • Auth Service ↔ MongoDB (user sessions, JWT)  
      • Clients ↔ WebSocket (for real‑time updates)  
      • Clients ↔ External (Mixpanel analytics, Canny feedback)  
      • CI/CD pipelines → build & publish packages, deploy services  

   c. Architectural patterns & design principles:  
      • Monorepo with “apps” (consumers) and “packages” (shared libs)  
      • Microservices for auth, API, and gateway  
      • Component‑driven development (Storybook)  
      • Layered slicing: adapters → containers → services → repositories  
      • Event‑driven: Kafka for decoupled notifications  
      • Single‑page application pattern in both desktop & web  

   d. Key technologies/frameworks:  
      • Frontend: Svelte, Vite, Storybook  
      • Desktop: Tauri, Rust  
      • Backend: NestJS, Mongoose, Kafka  
      • Infra: Docker, Docker Compose  
      • CI/CD: GitHub Actions, SonarQube  
      • Shared: TypeScript, Yarn workspaces  

5. Tailoring diagram to this full‑stack monorepo  
   • Highlight “apps” vs “packages” separation.  
   • Show how shared packages feed into desktop & web builds.  
   • Emphasize Docker Compose orchestration of backend services and local Mongo/Kafka.  
   • Show build pipelines per app in GitHub Actions.  

6. Diagramming guidelines  
   • Use distinct shapes or colors for:  
     – User‑facing clients (e.g., blue rectangles)  
     – Services/microservices (e.g., green rectangles)  
     – Data stores (e.g., cylinder icons)  
     – Shared libraries (e.g., folder icons)  
   • Label each box clearly with name + tech stack.  
   • Draw directional arrows to indicate request/response flows.  
   • Annotate key protocols (HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC if any).  
   • Legend explaining color/shape semantics.  

7. Detail & completeness  
   • Capture every “app” in the monorepo and its dependency on shared packages.  
   • Include backend services even though they live in separate repos—because Docker Compose in this repo brings them up.  
   • Show CI workflows that build and publish the design system, clients, and backend containers.  
   • Don’t overload: group related feature packages under a single “Shared UI Library” box, but call out major ones (@sparrow‑common, @sparrow‑library).  
   • Final diagram should let a new engineer understand at a glance:  
     – What runs where (desktop, web, backend)  
     – How components talk  
     – What shared code underpins them  
     – How infrastructure (Docker, CI/CD) stitches it all together.  
</explanation>
